passage:
"Neelam, it's almost midnight. Still on the essay?"
"Papa, it's due at eight. I've written one paragraph."
"Show me."
"It's bad. Manoj said he'll send me his from last year. Same topic."
Manoj Uncle's son had topped the class. Papa sat down. "And then?"
"And then I change some words."
"Would your teacher know?"
"Maybe not." She paused. "Maybe yes. She reads everything twice."
"And would you know?"
Neelam rolled her eyes. "Papa, don't do the philosophy thing."
"Fine. What's your one paragraph about?"
"How rivers shaped old towns." She looked at it again. "Actually, I had one more idea about the ghats."
"Write that. I'll make tea."
She groaned, but she deleted Manoj's message without opening it.

qa.q: What was Neelam's essay about?
qa.a: It was about how rivers shaped old towns.

qa.q: Why did Neelam roll her eyes at "And would you know?"
qa.a: She was tired and a bit defensive, but the question also pricked her, because she knew copying would feel dishonest to her.

qa.q: What worked about Papa's way of handling the temptation?
qa.a: He asked questions instead of lecturing, then turned her attention back to her own ideas and offered tea, so she chose not to copy.

qa.q: What would change if Neelam had used Manoj's essay?
qa.a: She might have finished faster but risked being caught, and she would have missed writing her own idea about the ghats.

grounding: It shows a teen tempted to copy an old essay late at night choosing to write her own with a parent's gentle questions.

passage: Last term I almost handed in an essay I didn't write. I'm Parveen. The topic was on the causes of the First World War, and I had three other tests that week. My classmate Nikita showed me how an AI tool could produce a full essay in a minute. It looked perfect. I pasted mine in, read it, and felt nothing. It didn't sound like me at all. It had words I'd never use. Then I thought about Ma'am's comment on my last essay: "I like how you argue." This one didn't argue anything. So I closed it and wrote my own at 1 am. It was messier. Ma'am gave it a B and wrote, "Your voice is back." Nikita got caught. I felt sorry for her, honestly.

qa.q: What grade did Parveen's essay get?
qa.a: It got a B.

qa.q: Why did Parveen feel nothing reading the AI-written essay?
qa.a: It didn't sound like her or carry her own arguments, so it felt empty and not really hers.

qa.q: What helped Parveen resist the shortcut?
qa.a: Remembering her teacher's praise for how she argues reminded her that her own voice was worth more than a perfect-looking copy.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel after getting caught?
qa.a: She is probably embarrassed and worried, and may wish she had written her own even if it was messier.

grounding: A teen reflects on resisting an AI-written essay and valuing her own original voice.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 9:
During the science project week, I noticed that Zubin's report looked very similar to Ishita's from the other section. Same diagrams, same unusual phrases. I spoke to both separately. Ishita was upset; she had lent her notebook to Zubin to "get an idea." Zubin admitted he had copied large parts. He looked at the floor and said, "I didn't think it was a big deal."
I explained that it wasn't fair to Ishita, and that the project was meant to help him learn, not just produce a report. I gave him three extra days to redo it himself and asked him to apologise to Ishita.
Follow-up: His new report was shorter but his own. Ishita said they're still friends.

qa.q: How many extra days did the teacher give Zubin?
qa.a: The teacher gave him three extra days.

qa.q: What does Zubin looking at the floor suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt ashamed once he was caught, even though he claimed he didn't think it was a big deal.

qa.q: What was fair about the teacher's response?
qa.a: She spoke to each student privately, explained why copying mattered, and gave Zubin a chance to redo the work and repair things with Ishita.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt when she learned her notebook was copied?
qa.a: She probably felt used and upset, since she only meant to help, and worried she might be blamed too.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teen caught copying, understanding why originality matters and redoing the work.

passage:
Week one: Urmila volunteered to organise the Class 10 charity sale. She made a list of jobs and handed them out. By Friday, nobody had done anything. She did most of it herself and snapped at Pranav in the corridor.

Week two: Pranav stopped her after class. "You didn't ask what we wanted to do. You just told us." Urmila was stung, but she listened. At the next meeting, she asked people to choose their jobs. Pranav picked posters; he was good at drawing.

Week four: The sale ran out of samosas by noon. Someone had counted wrong. The principal asked who was in charge. Urmila swallowed. "Me. I checked the numbers and missed it." Pranav stood beside her.

qa.q: What job did Pranav choose?
qa.a: He picked posters because he was good at drawing.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel when Pranav said she just told people what to do?
qa.a: She was stung and a bit hurt, but chose to listen, showing she wanted the project to work more than she wanted to be right.

qa.q: What changed in Urmila's leadership, and why did it work?
qa.a: She let people choose their own jobs, which gave them ownership, and she took the blame openly when the samosa count failed.

qa.q: How might Pranav see Urmila after she took the blame?
qa.a: He probably respected her more, which is why he stood beside her, since she didn't point fingers at others.

grounding: It shows a teen leader learning over weeks to motivate peers and take responsibility for a failure.

passage: Samir, beta, you've been made sports captain, so let me tell you about your Reena Didi. When she was in Class 11, she was the head of the school's science club. The first year she wanted everything perfect, so she did all the work herself. The others got bored and stopped coming. She came home crying. "Nobody helps me," she said. I asked her, "Did you ask them? Or did you do it before they could?" She was quiet for a long time. Next term she gave each member a small experiment to run and only helped when asked. One experiment failed at the school exhibition, and she stood up and said, "That's my fault, I didn't check the wiring." That's the day they started trusting her.

qa.q: What was Reena Didi the head of in Class 11?
qa.a: She was the head of the school's science club.

qa.q: Why did Reena Didi come home crying the first year?
qa.a: She felt alone and frustrated because the others had stopped coming, and she believed nobody would help her.

qa.q: What could Samir learn from Reena Didi's second term?
qa.a: He could give teammates real responsibilities, support them only when asked, and own mistakes openly so they trust him.

qa.q: How might the club members have seen Reena when she took the blame?
qa.a: They likely saw her as fair and brave, someone who protects the team rather than blaming them, so they began trusting her.

grounding: An elder tells a younger relative how a teen leader learned to share work and take blame when something failed.

passage: The science fair was two days away, and the school's power had gone for a day because of a storm. Sharmila, team leader for Class 9's solar model, had to reorganise everything. Her friend Kavitha was supposed to finish the panel, but she had fever and was home. Sharmila gathered the other three members in the dim classroom with a torch. "Okay. We've lost a day and a person. What can we still do well?" They split the work: one on wiring, one on posters, one on the talk. Sharmila called Kavitha to check on her and to ask how she'd planned the angles. On the day, the model worked, but one poster was crooked. The judge asked who made it. Sharmila said, "We rushed it. That's on me."

qa.q: Why was Kavitha unable to finish the panel?
qa.a: She had fever and was at home.

qa.q: What might Sharmila have been feeling in the dim classroom?
qa.a: She was probably stressed and worried about the lost day and missing member, but she stayed calm to keep the team focused.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do that helped the team under pressure?
qa.a: She asked what they could still do well, split tasks clearly, stayed in touch with Kavitha, and took responsibility for the crooked poster.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel about Sharmila's phone call?
qa.a: She may feel cared for and still included, even though she was sick and couldn't be there.

grounding: It shows a teen leader organising peers under time pressure and taking blame for a flaw.

passage:
"Arohi, why do you talk like that on the phone?"
"Like what, Indu?"
"All 'yaar' and 'chill' with your friends. With Nani you speak Marathi like a priest."
Arohi laughed. "Because Nani would faint if I said 'chill.'"
"So which one is the real you?"
Arohi stopped folding clothes. She thought about it. "Both?" she said. "At school I used to hide the Marathi. Someone laughed at my accent in Class 7."
"And now?"
"Now I taught three girls the Marathi word for 'annoying.' They use it all the time."
Indu grinned. "What is it?"
"I'm not telling you. You'll use it on me."
"Aai says you sound like her when you're angry."
Arohi smiled. "Good."

qa.q: What did Arohi teach three girls at school?
qa.a: She taught them the Marathi word for "annoying."

qa.q: What does Arohi's "Good" at the end suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she's proud of sounding like her mother and now feels comfortable with her home language rather than ashamed of it.

qa.q: What helped Arohi move from hiding her Marathi to sharing it?
qa.a: Sharing a fun word with friends turned her language into something others enjoyed, instead of something to be laughed at.

qa.q: How might Indu see her older sister's switching between languages?
qa.a: She seems curious and slightly teasing, but she also learns that switching can be natural, not fake.

grounding: It shows a teen moving between home, school and friend language with growing pride instead of shame.

passage: When I moved from Kochi to Delhi in Class 8, I stopped speaking Malayalam outside the house. I'm Joseph. At my new school, a boy imitated my accent in the canteen, and everyone laughed. So I copied the way the Delhi boys talked, their slang, the way they said "bhai." At home, Amma would ask me something in Malayalam and I'd answer in Hindi. She never said anything, but I saw her face. Then last year my friend Lalit came over for lunch. Amma made appam and stew. Lalit ate three and begged for the recipe. He asked me to teach him Malayalam words. I felt proud, and weirdly relieved. Now I switch without thinking much. Different rooms, different voices, same me.

qa.q: What did Amma make when Lalit came for lunch?
qa.a: She made appam and stew.

qa.q: What might Amma have felt when Joseph answered her in Hindi?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt or sad that her son seemed to be pulling away from their language, though she didn't say it.

qa.q: What helped Joseph feel proud of his heritage again?
qa.a: Seeing a friend enjoy his mother's food and want to learn Malayalam showed him his culture could be admired, not mocked.

qa.q: How might Lalit see Joseph's switching between languages?
qa.a: He probably sees it as interesting and even cool, a sign that Joseph belongs in more than one world.

grounding: A teen reflects on hiding his home language after mockery and regaining pride while switching between cultures.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 10:
Kashish asked to see me after an incident in the class group chat. She had posted a photo from her cousin's wedding, wearing a traditional outfit, and someone commented, "Village vibes." She deleted the photo. In our session she said she felt like two people: one at home with Punjabi songs and big family dinners, one at school trying to seem "cool." I asked what she liked about each. She smiled about the dinners.
We talked about how moving between groups is normal, and how she could choose what to share. Her friend Keerthana, from another state, told her she loved the photo.
Follow-up: Kashish reposted it with the caption "My people." I've told the class teacher about the comment.

qa.q: What caption did Kashish use when she reposted the photo?
qa.a: She used the caption "My people."

qa.q: How did Kashish feel after the "Village vibes" comment?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and split, like two different people, which is why she deleted the photo.

qa.q: What in the counsellor's approach helped Kashish?
qa.a: Asking what she liked about each part of her life, and saying moving between groups is normal, helped her feel she didn't have to hide one side.

qa.q: How might Keerthana's comment have affected Kashish?
qa.a: Hearing that a friend loved the photo probably made her feel accepted and gave her courage to repost it. 🙂

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teen moving from shame to pride about her home culture after an online comment.

passage: Arnab, you asked why I get upset when people say "these migrants." Let me tell you about Zainab. When I was your age, she joined our school in Kolkata. Her family had come from across the border after floods took their fields. The other kids called her names. I didn't join in, but I didn't stop them either. One day we had a geography project on rivers, and she was put in my group. She knew everything about how the delta shifts, how floods move people. She told us about her grandfather's boat. I realised I'd been scared of her without knowing anything. After that I asked her questions. We're still friends. So when you hear "these migrants," ask who they are first.

qa.q: What had taken Zainab's family's fields?
qa.a: Floods had taken their fields.

qa.q: How did the speaker feel about Zainab before the geography project?
qa.a: They were scared of her without really knowing her, and felt uneasy about not stopping the name-calling.

qa.q: What advice does the speaker give Arnab, and why is it useful?
qa.a: To ask who migrants are before judging, because curiosity replaces fear and stereotypes with real people's stories.

qa.q: How might Zainab have felt when her classmate started asking questions?
qa.a: She probably felt seen and less alone, after being called names by others.

grounding: An elder uses a memory of a migrant classmate to teach curiosity over prejudice.

passage: Dolma had one week to finish her school project on migration, and the only person she could interview was Yash, the new boy whose family had moved from a town in Nepal. The problem: Yash barely spoke, and the library's internet was down. Dolma waited after class. "Can I ask you some questions? For the project?" Yash looked wary. "Why?" "Because I only know what's in the textbook," she said honestly. He hesitated, then shrugged. For three lunch breaks they sat on the steps. He told her about the long bus journey, missing his grandmother, learning Hindi from cartoons. Dolma realised some classmates' jokes about him were plain cruel. In her presentation, she used his words, with his permission, and the class went quiet.

qa.q: Where did Yash's family move from?
qa.a: They moved from a town in Nepal.

qa.q: Why did Yash look wary at first?
qa.a: He may have expected to be mocked or used, since some classmates had joked about him, so he wasn't sure Dolma's interest was genuine.

qa.q: What helped Dolma get Yash to open up?
qa.a: She was honest about only knowing the textbook and gave him time over three lunch breaks, which showed real curiosity rather than judgement.

qa.q: How might the class see Yash after the presentation?
qa.a: Some may see him as a real person with a story now, and feel uncomfortable about their earlier jokes.

grounding: It shows a teen learning about migration and prejudice through curious, honest conversations with a classmate.

passage: Gargi's colony in Bengaluru had a new family on the third floor, from Afghanistan. Some neighbours whispered at the gate. Gargi's friend Gurleen said her mother had told her to "be careful." Gargi wasn't sure what that meant. At the building's Holi, the new family's daughter stood at the edge with a plate of sweets she had brought. Nobody took one. Gargi walked over and took two. "What are these?" she asked. The girl explained they were from Kabul, made for celebrations. Gurleen came over, a bit slowly, and tried one. "It's like a cousin of our barfi," she said. The girl laughed. Later, Gargi asked her mother why people were whispering. Her mother said, "People fear what they don't know."

qa.q: Where was the new family from?
qa.a: They were from Afghanistan.

qa.q: Why might Gurleen have walked over slowly?
qa.a: She may have felt unsure because of her mother's warning, but curiosity and seeing Gargi go first pulled her in.

qa.q: What did Gargi's choice at Holi do well?
qa.a: By taking the sweets and asking a question, she broke the awkward silence and made space for the new girl to share her culture.

qa.q: What would change if nobody had taken a sweet?
qa.a: The new girl would likely have felt rejected and alone, and the whispers might have hardened into lasting prejudice.

grounding: It shows teens overcoming neighbours' prejudice towards a migrant family through curiosity at a festival.

subtype: Handling Failure, Result Disappointment & Family Crisis
passage: I'm Vinita, and Irfan sits next to me in class. When the pre-board results came, he got the lowest marks in our section in maths. He laughed and said, "Whatever," but he didn't eat his lunch. The next week I heard that his father's shop had closed. He came to school with the same shirt three days running. He stopped joking. I didn't know what to say. Then one day I saw him in the library with a stack of old question papers, doing them one by one. He asked the maths teacher to check his work after school. He looked tired, but he kept going. I don't know how he really feels. But he told me, "I can't fix everything. I can fix this."

qa.q: What did Irfan do in the library?
qa.a: He worked through a stack of old question papers one by one.

qa.q: What does Irfan's "Whatever" alongside his untouched lunch suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was hurt and worried by the result but trying to hide it behind a careless word.

qa.q: How could a teacher support someone like Irfan?
qa.a: A teacher could check his work, as the maths teacher did, and quietly ask how he's doing, pointing him to the counsellor if home is hard.

qa.q: How might Vinita be affected by watching Irfan?
qa.a: She seems worried and unsure what to say, but also moved and hopeful seeing him keep going.

grounding: A classmate observes a teen coping with a bad result and a family financial crisis without losing hope.

subtype: Handling Failure, Result Disappointment & Family Crisis
passage:
Before: The night Vasudha's parents had their worst fight, she lay awake listening to raised voices through the wall. The next morning she failed a chemistry test she had studied for. At lunch, her friend Gurpreet asked if she was okay. Vasudha said, "Fine," and went to the washroom to cry.

During: A few days later, Gurpreet sat next to her on the bus home and simply said, "You don't have to tell me. I'm just here." Vasudha told her everything.

After: The next week, Vasudha talked to the school counsellor. Her parents were still arguing, but she learned that it wasn't her fault. She retook the chemistry test and passed. "One thing at a time," she wrote in her notebook.

qa.q: Where did Vasudha tell Gurpreet everything?
qa.a: She told her on the bus home.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha say "Fine" and then cry in the washroom?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and ashamed about her family's fighting and didn't feel ready to share it in public.

qa.q: What made Gurpreet's second approach work?
qa.a: She didn't push for details and simply offered to be there, which made Vasudha feel safe enough to open up.

qa.q: How might Vasudha's parents feel if they knew their fighting affected her test?
qa.a: They would likely feel sorry and worried, and it might push them to protect her from their conflict.

grounding: It shows a teen coping over several days with parental conflict and a failed test while keeping hope.

subtype: Handling Failure, Result Disappointment & Family Crisis
passage: Disha, you know your cousin Deepika? When she was sixteen, her father lost his job. That year she failed her board exam in science. Everyone in the family was upset, and her mother cried in the kitchen. Deepika told me she felt like the whole house was falling. But here's what she did. She took a part-time job at the photocopy shop to help, and she registered to retake the exam. She studied at night with the lamp near the shop counter. Some days she wanted to give up. She told me once, "Chachi, I can't see the end." I told her, "You don't have to see it. Just see tomorrow." She passed the next year. Now she's a nurse. She still keeps that lamp.

qa.q: Where did Deepika take a part-time job?
qa.a: She took a job at the photocopy shop.

qa.q: What does Deepika saying "I can't see the end" reveal about how she felt?
qa.a: It reveals she felt exhausted and close to losing hope under the weight of the failed exam and family money troubles.

qa.q: What could Disha take from Deepika's story when things go wrong?
qa.a: She could focus on one day at a time and take small, practical steps, like retaking an exam, instead of trying to fix everything at once.

qa.q: How might Deepika's mother have felt watching her daughter work and study?
qa.a: She might have felt both guilty and proud, sad about the hardship but moved by her daughter's strength.

grounding: An elder tells a younger relative how a teen coped with failure and financial hardship while holding on to hope.

passage: Jahnavi, come, sit. You keep saying you're stupid because reading is slow for you. Let me tell you about your uncle Harish. When he was in school, the letters on the page used to jump around, and he read slowly. Teachers called him lazy. He believed them. In Class 9 a new teacher noticed he could explain the whole science chapter aloud, but couldn't write it fast. She suggested an assessment, and the specialist said his brain handled reading differently. That word, "differently," changed everything for him. He asked for extra time in exams, and he listened to audio books. He still reads slowly. But he's an engineer now, and the best at explaining things in his office. You're not stupid. You just need to find what works for you.

qa.q: What could Harish do well that the new teacher noticed?
qa.a: He could explain the whole science chapter aloud.

qa.q: How did the word "differently" change how Harish felt about himself?
qa.a: It replaced the label of lazy with an understanding of how his brain worked, which lifted his shame and gave him hope.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi try, based on Harish's story?
qa.a: She could notice what helps her, like listening or explaining aloud, and ask a teacher about support such as an assessment or extra time.

qa.q: How might Harish's first teachers see him now?
qa.a: They might feel regret for calling him lazy, realising they missed his real strengths.

grounding: An elder tells a younger relative about recognising a reading difference, finding strengths and asking for support.

passage: The exam hall was stuffy, and Ishita's chair creaked every time she moved. The fans hummed, someone kept clicking a pen, and the invigilator's shoes squeaked. Ishita had always found noise harder than others did. Every sound pulled at her attention. She read the first question three times and couldn't take it in. Her panic grew. She raised her hand. "Ma'am, can I sit near the back, away from the fan?" The invigilator hesitated, then let her move. Ishita put her hands over her ears for a minute and breathed slowly. Afterwards, she told her friend Siddharth, "I think I need to ask for a quiet room next time." Siddharth said, "Talk to the counsellor. My cousin got that."

qa.q: Where did Ishita ask to sit?
qa.a: She asked to sit near the back, away from the fan.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when she read the first question three times?
qa.a: She was panicking because the noises kept pulling her attention and she couldn't take the words in.

qa.q: What did Ishita do that helped, and what else could she try?
qa.a: She asked to move and calmed herself by covering her ears and breathing; next, she could talk to the counsellor about a quiet room.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see Ishita's request for a quiet room?
qa.a: He sees it as normal and reasonable, since his cousin got one, which may help Ishita feel less odd for asking.

grounding: It shows a teen recognising her sensitivity to noise during an exam and asking for support.

passage: In their Mumbai flat, Pradeep's younger sister Maria sat at the dining table surrounded by open notebooks, all half-filled. She was fifteen and could start five things at once but finish none. Pradeep, home from college, watched her jump up to get water, then check her phone, then start a new page. "I'm hopeless," she muttered. Pradeep sat down. "You're not hopeless. You're really good at ideas. Remember your science model?" She nodded slowly. "So what if we try short bursts? Ten minutes, then a stretch." They tried. She got one page done and grinned. Later she said she wanted to talk to her class teacher about her attention. "Maybe there are other tricks," she said. Pradeep thought that was brave.

qa.q: How long did Pradeep suggest each work burst should be?
qa.a: He suggested ten minutes, then a stretch.

qa.q: Why did Maria mutter "I'm hopeless"?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and ashamed at starting many things but finishing none, and blamed herself.

qa.q: What made Pradeep's response helpful?
qa.a: He reminded her of a real strength, then offered a practical strategy that fit her attention, instead of criticising her.

qa.q: Why might Pradeep think Maria's plan to talk to her teacher is brave?
qa.a: Asking for help means admitting she struggles, which can feel exposing, but it shows she's taking her needs seriously.

grounding: It shows a teen recognising her attention difficulties and strengths and deciding to ask for support.

passage: In Marseille, Leila and her cousin Layla were given a school project: reduce your family's carbon footprint for a month. Leila rolled her eyes. "One family won't save the planet." Layla, who had read more, explained that most warming came from burning coal, oil and gas for power and transport. "So small things add up if lots of people do them. And we can push the school too." They made a list: walk or cycle to school, turn off lights, eat fewer takeaway meals in plastic. Leila's father grumbled about the bus. At the end of the month, their class wrote to the town council asking for a safer bike lane. Leila was surprised how good it felt to sign her name.

qa.q: What did the cousins' class write to the town council about?
qa.a: They asked for a safer bike lane.

qa.q: How did Leila feel at the start of the project, and how did that change?
qa.a: She was doubtful and dismissive, rolling her eyes, but by the end she felt surprised and good about taking part.

qa.q: What made the cousins' approach realistic?
qa.a: They picked small personal steps and also joined a group action, the letter to the council, which could make a bigger difference.

qa.q: How might Leila's father see the changes?
qa.a: He grumbled about the bus, suggesting he found them inconvenient, but he might come round if he sees the girls' effort.

grounding: It shows teens learning the causes of climate change and taking realistic personal and group action.

passage: The school's eco-club in Pune had a new project: cut the canteen's waste. Vaibhav, Class 10, thought it would be boring. His friend Bhupen had checked how much food was thrown away each day and brought a photo of the overflowing bins. "That's rotting food making methane," Bhupen said. "It warms the planet more than we think." Vaibhav looked at the photo for a long time. They met the canteen manager, who was worried about losing money. Bhupen suggested smaller portions with free refills. The manager agreed to try it for two weeks. The bins got lighter. Vaibhav started a compost pit behind the science lab. He didn't like getting his hands dirty, but he liked the numbers going down.

qa.q: What did Bhupen say rotting food makes?
qa.a: He said it makes methane.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav look at the photo for a long time?
qa.a: Seeing the overflowing bins made the problem feel real and changed his view that the project would be boring.

qa.q: What made Bhupen's suggestion to the canteen manager workable?
qa.a: Smaller portions with free refills addressed the manager's worry about money while cutting waste.

qa.q: How might the canteen manager see the project after two weeks?
qa.a: He might be pleased to see less waste and no loss, and more open to the students' next idea.

grounding: It shows teens understanding a cause of climate change and taking practical group action at school.

passage:
Dear Eshaan,
You asked me why I've stopped asking Papa to drive me to tuition. Honestly, it's the climate project we did in school. I learned that cars burning petrol are one of the big reasons the earth is heating up. At first I felt scared and hopeless. What can I even do? But our teacher said we can't fix it alone, but we can do our part and push for bigger changes.
So now I cycle to tuition, I carry a steel bottle, and our class is asking the principal for solar lights on the terrace.
I know you think it's too small. Maybe it is. But it feels better than doing nothing. 🙂 Come cycling with me on Sunday?
Vinita

qa.q: What is Vinita's class asking the principal for?
qa.a: They are asking for solar lights on the terrace.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel when she first learned about climate change?
qa.a: She felt scared and hopeless, unsure what she could do.

qa.q: Why is Vinita's mix of actions a sensible response?
qa.a: She takes small personal steps like cycling and also joins a group request, which is realistic without being overwhelming.

qa.q: If you were Eshaan, how might you respond to Vinita's invitation?
qa.a: You might still think it's small, but joining her for a cycle ride could be a fun first step.

grounding: A teen's letter explains the causes of climate change she learned and the realistic actions she is taking.

passage:
"Dolma, you ate chips for breakfast?"
"Yogesh, mind your business."
"You said you were going to start running."
"I did. On Monday."
"It's Thursday."
Dolma threw a cushion at her brother. "I got tired. And bored. And my shoes hurt."
"So get new shoes. Or walk. You don't have to run like a crazy person."
"You're one to talk. You only play video games."
"Okay, deal. I'll walk with you if you eat real breakfast."
"Fine. Poha tomorrow. And you have to walk every day, not just when you feel like it."
"Every day?"
"Every day. Even if it's ten minutes."
The next morning they walked around the colony twice. Dolma complained the whole way, but she laughed more than she expected.

qa.q: What did Dolma eat for breakfast?
qa.a: She ate chips.

qa.q: Why did Dolma stop running after Monday?
qa.a: She felt tired, bored and her shoes hurt, so the plan she started with enthusiasm quickly felt too hard to keep up.

qa.q: What made the siblings' new plan more likely to last?
qa.a: They chose a smaller goal, walking even ten minutes every day, made a deal to keep each other going, and swapped chips for a real breakfast.

qa.q: How might Yogesh feel about walking every day?
qa.a: He may grumble, since he mostly plays video games, but joining his sister could make it fun for him too.

grounding: It shows siblings building consistent exercise and eating habits by making small, shared commitments.

passage: Last summer I decided to get fit, and I went at it like a crazy person. I'm Anirban. I ran every morning for an hour and skipped rice because some video said carbs were bad. By the second week my knees hurt, I was cranky, and I fell asleep in class. My friend Chinmay, who's on the football team, laughed at me, but kindly. He said his coach told them to build up slowly and eat properly, not cut whole foods. So I started again. Three short runs a week, stretching, rice and dal like normal. It felt too easy at first. But I didn't quit this time. Now, a year later, I run twice as far, and I still eat rice.

qa.q: How many short runs a week did Anirban start with the second time?
qa.a: He started with three short runs a week.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel after his first two weeks?
qa.a: He was in pain, cranky and exhausted, which shows the extreme plan was hurting rather than helping him.

qa.q: Why did Anirban's second approach work better?
qa.a: Building up slowly and eating normally was sustainable, so he didn't burn out and kept going for a year.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel seeing Anirban's progress a year later?
qa.a: He'd probably feel pleased that his coach's advice helped and proud of his friend's consistency. 👍

grounding: A teen reflects on replacing an extreme fitness plan with a consistent, balanced routine.

passage:
PE teacher's note, Class 9:
Thomas has been skipping PE for three weeks, saying he forgot his kit. His classmate Karthik mentioned Thomas said he's "bad at sports" and doesn't want to be laughed at. I spoke to Thomas privately. He admitted he gets out of breath fast and felt embarrassed. I explained fitness is built slowly and that everyone starts somewhere. We agreed he'd try skipping rope, which he enjoys, for a few minutes each lesson, building up weekly. I also talked about drinking water, sleep and eating proper meals, not just snacks. I asked Karthik to partner with him.
Follow-up: Thomas has come to four lessons in a row. He still gets out of breath, but he's smiling more.

qa.q: What activity did Thomas agree to try?
qa.a: He agreed to try skipping rope.

qa.q: Why was Thomas skipping PE?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about getting out of breath and feared being laughed at, so he used forgotten kit as an excuse.

qa.q: What made the teacher's plan work for Thomas?
qa.a: He spoke privately, chose an activity Thomas enjoys, built it up slowly, and paired him with Karthik for support.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel being asked to partner with Thomas?
qa.a: He might feel trusted and glad to help, since he already noticed Thomas was struggling.

grounding: A PE teacher's note shows helping a teen build a consistent fitness habit and healthy eating.

passage: The school's philosophy club had one hour before the debate, and the power had gone out, so Sonali and Ganga sat in the dark library with a single torch. Their topic: "Is it ever right to lie?" Sonali, who liked rules, said lying is always wrong; her grandmother's faith said so. Ganga argued that lying to protect someone could be right, like hiding a friend from danger. "So which is it?" Sonali asked, frustrated. Ganga shrugged. "Different systems answer differently. One says follow the rule. One says look at the results." Sonali thought for a while. "Maybe both help. Rules keep us honest, but we should also think about who gets hurt." They agreed to present both views fairly. The torch flickered.

qa.q: What was the topic of the debate?
qa.a: The topic was "Is it ever right to lie?"

qa.q: Why did Sonali get frustrated?
qa.a: She believed strongly that lying is always wrong, and Ganga's example challenged that certainty, making her uneasy.

qa.q: What made Sonali and Ganga's final approach reasonable?
qa.a: They compared the rule-based view and the results-based view and chose to present both fairly, instead of mocking one side.

qa.q: How might Sonali's grandmother react to the girls' conclusion?
qa.a: She might still stress honesty but appreciate that Sonali is thinking carefully about when harm is involved.

grounding: It shows teens comparing rule-based and results-based ethics reasonably under time pressure.

passage: Shankar's father was a temple priest, and Akash's family didn't follow any religion. They were best friends in a Chennai school. One evening, walking home past the temple, Akash asked, "How do you know God exists?" Shankar felt his face get hot. "How do you know he doesn't?" They argued all the way to the bus stop. Then Akash laughed. "We're both just saying the same thing louder." Shankar grinned, still a bit annoyed. The next week, their philosophy teacher explained arguments for and against, and how people's beliefs shape how they live. Shankar still believed; Akash still didn't. But they started asking each other real questions instead of trying to win. They now meet at the tea stall on Fridays to talk.

qa.q: What was Shankar's father's job?
qa.a: He was a temple priest.

qa.q: Why did Shankar's face get hot when Akash asked his question?
qa.a: He felt his faith and his family were being challenged, which made him defensive and a little hurt.

qa.q: What changed in how the friends discussed beliefs?
qa.a: They stopped trying to win and started asking genuine questions, which let them understand each other while keeping their own views.

qa.q: How might Akash feel when Shankar talks about his faith now?
qa.a: He might feel curious and respectful, seeing Shankar's belief as something to understand, not defeat.

grounding: It shows teens comparing religious belief and non-belief reasonably and respectfully.

passage:
"Kamal, why are you reading that thick book at dinner?"
"It's philosophy, Ma. Different ideas of how to be good."
"And?"
"And some say follow duty. Some say do what makes most people happy. Some say be a good character."
Jomon, his older brother, snorted. "Which one's right?"
"I don't know yet. That's the point."
"Our religion already tells us."
"I know. And it has good ideas. I'm just seeing what others say."
Ma put down the ladle. "As long as you respect other people's answers too."
"I'm trying. It's hard when Jomon's being annoying."
Jomon laughed. "Fine. Tell me one idea. I'll argue."
"Deal. But no shouting."
"No promises."

qa.q: What was Kamal reading at dinner?
qa.a: He was reading a thick philosophy book about different ideas of how to be good.

qa.q: What does Kamal's "I don't know yet. That's the point" reveal about his attitude?
qa.a: It shows he's curious and open, enjoying the search rather than rushing to a final answer.

qa.q: How could Kamal and Jomon make their debate useful?
qa.a: They could take one idea at a time, argue calmly without shouting, and respect each other's reasons.

qa.q: How does Ma seem to see Kamal's reading?
qa.a: She seems accepting but a little careful, wanting him to explore while respecting others' answers.

grounding: It shows a teen comparing ethical systems and religion reasonably in a family conversation.

passage: I'm Alka. My friend Nandini decided in January to learn the guitar by her birthday in July. At first she practised every evening; I could hear her through the wall. By February, the sound stopped for days. When I asked, she said, "My fingers hurt and it's boring. Same chords again and again." In March she broke a string and didn't replace it for two weeks. I thought she'd quit. Then she started playing again, only fifteen minutes each night, and marking a calendar with ticks. Some days she only played one song badly. By June she could play three songs. On her birthday she played for her family, and her hands shook. I don't know what kept her going, but the calendar was full of ticks.

qa.q: When did Nandini want to learn the guitar by?
qa.a: She wanted to learn by her birthday in July.

qa.q: What does Nandini's broken string left for two weeks suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was discouraged and losing motivation, close to giving up.

qa.q: What helped Nandini keep going after the boring months?
qa.a: Shorter daily practice and a calendar of ticks made the goal feel manageable and showed her progress.

qa.q: How might Alka feel hearing Nandini play on her birthday?
qa.a: She'd likely feel proud and surprised, since she had thought Nandini would quit. 🎉

grounding: A friend observes a teen sustaining effort on a months-long goal despite boredom and setbacks.

passage:
January: Omkar and his friend Salma started a school project to map every tree in their neighbourhood. They were excited and made a big chart.

March: The chart had forty trees. Then exams came, and rain washed out two Saturdays. Salma said she was bored of counting leaves. Omkar felt the same but hated leaving things half-done. They agreed to do just five trees a week.

June: They had mapped 120 trees. One day the municipality cut down three for a road. Salma was angry, and Omkar felt like the whole thing was pointless. Then the school principal asked to see their map for a meeting about green spaces. They printed it proudly.

qa.q: How many trees had they mapped by June?
qa.a: They had mapped 120 trees.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when the municipality cut down three trees?
qa.a: He felt the whole project was pointless, discouraged that their work couldn't protect the trees.

qa.q: What helped Omkar and Salma keep going through boredom and exams?
qa.a: They lowered the goal to five trees a week, which made steady progress possible.

qa.q: What would change if the principal hadn't asked for their map?
qa.a: They might have stayed discouraged and quit, not seeing that their long effort could be useful.

grounding: It shows teens keeping up a multi-month project through boredom and setbacks.

passage: Avni, let me tell you something about your Leela Didi. When she was fifteen, she wanted to write a whole novel. Everyone laughed. "A novel? You can't even finish your homework." She wrote one page every night. Some nights it was just half a page, and she complained it was rubbish. After three months, she was bored and wanted to stop. I told her, "Then write boring pages. Just write." She laughed, but she kept going. Around the sixth month she lost a whole chapter when her notebook got wet in the monsoon. She cried for a day. Then she started it again, and she said the new one was better. She finished in a year. It's still on my shelf. Your turn now, beta.

qa.q: What happened to Leela Didi's chapter around the sixth month?
qa.a: She lost a whole chapter when her notebook got wet in the monsoon.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when she lost the chapter?
qa.a: She was heartbroken and cried for a day, but then found the resolve to start again.

qa.q: What can Avni learn from Leela's approach?
qa.a: Small daily effort, even on boring days, and restarting after a setback can carry a long project to the end.

qa.q: How might Leela's family see her finished novel now?
qa.a: They likely feel proud and a bit sheepish about laughing, seeing it on the shelf as proof of her persistence.

grounding: An elder tells a younger relative how a teen sustained a year-long project through boredom and setbacks.
